articles.title: Tech Life - School deepfake ransoms - BBC Sounds
articles.summary: For years, schools have posted photos of their pupils online. But could they be misused?
articles.body:
World Service , · 11 Aug 2026 , · 26 mins

For many schools, it’s normal to post pictures of their own pupils online, either celebrating events or for marketing. But these photos could also be taken by criminals and used to make distressing deepfake AI images. We speak to the founder of a company which says it has a solution. Also on the programme, the incredible ways graphene can augment our senses – including to smell for diseases. And the student with dyslexia who invented his own tech to help him through his course. Presenter: Chris Vallance Producer: Imran Rahman-Jones (Image: A child places a metal pin impression toy over their face, so they cannot be identified. Credit: Getty Images)

articles.title: Fun fact: Dolly Parton wrote most of 'Coat of Many Colors' on a dry-cleaning receipt
articles.summary: Did you know that "Coat of Many Colors" was born on a receipt, and that a distant exoplanet has clouds made of small quartz crystals?
articles.body:
Fun fact: Dolly Parton wrote most of 'Coat of Many Colors' on a dry-cleaning receipt Did you know that "Coat of Many Colors" was born on a receipt, and that a distant exoplanet has clouds made of small quartz crystals? Start Slideshow

Did you know that "Coat of Many Colors" was born on a receipt, and that a distant exoplanet has clouds made of small quartz crystals?

While touring with Porter Wagoner, Dolly Parton was on a bus when the words to "Coat of Many Colors" began flowing, and she had nothing to write on. She grabbed a dry-cleaning tag from one of Wagoner’s outfits and wrote the majority of the song’s lyrics on the receipt, she said in an interview with the Library of Congress.

NASA's James Webb Space Telescope detected evidence of quartz nanocrystals in the high-altitude clouds of WASP-17 b, a scorching gas giant about 1,300 light-years away. The crystals are only about 10 nanometers across and appear to form directly from gas in the planet's atmosphere rather than being swept up from a rocky surface. It was the first detection of silica particles in an exoplanet atmosphere.

Sea otters can have up to one million hairs per square inch, giving them the densest fur of any animal. Unlike most marine mammals, they lack a thick layer of insulating blubber, so their coat traps air against the skin to keep cold ocean water away.

Bottlenose dolphins develop individually distinctive calls known as signature whistles, which broadcast the identity of the caller. Researchers have found that these whistles are learned early in life and their basic patterns can remain stable for decades. Dolphins can even copy the signature whistles of close companions, potentially using them to address specific individuals.

In 1945, Raytheon engineer Percy Spencer noticed that a candy/chocolate bar in his pocket had melted while he was working near an active magnetron, a device used in radar equipment. That observation prompted him to experiment with foods such as popcorn and helped lead to the development of the microwave oven.

On Jan. 28, 1896, Walter Arnold was caught driving about 8 mph through Paddock Wood, England, where the speed limit was 2 mph. Guinness World Records identifies the case as the first recorded speeding fine, while The Independent describes it as the first speeding conviction.

Researchers observed two sacoglossan sea slug species detach their heads from bodies containing the heart and other major organs. Younger individuals regenerated complete replacement bodies, including new hearts, in about three weeks. The team proposed that chloroplasts retained from algae may help sustain the detached heads, but that mechanism remains unconfirmed.

Scientists detected hematite — an iron oxide commonly called rust — at high latitudes on the Moon, despite its lack of breathable oxygen and liquid water. Researchers propose that oxygen escaping Earth's upper atmosphere may reach the lunar surface, while trace water and dust impacts help drive oxidation.

Researchers illuminated three preserved platypus specimens with ultraviolet light and found that their brown fur fluoresced blue-green. The glow results from the fur absorbing invisible UV wavelengths and re-emitting visible light, though its biological purpose remains unknown.

Carl Mayer, nephew of Oscar Mayer, created the first Wienermobile in 1936. The Wisconsin Historical Society says the original "Wiener Wagon" promoted the company’s Yellow Band German Wiener—a giant edible-looking billboard designed for the road.

In December 1868, the world's first traffic signal was installed outside London's Houses of Parliament, using semaphore arms by day and red and green gas lamps at night. Less than a month later, a leaking gas line caused it to explode and badly burned the officer operating it.

Many toothpastes contain sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS), a foaming detergent that temporarily reduces sweetness perception and alters how taste receptors respond. Orange juice itself does not become more bitter; its sweetness is muted, making its naturally acidic and bitter notes seem much stronger.

Archaeologists found two interlocking, intentionally notched logs at Kalambo Falls in Zambia, dated to at least 476,000 years ago. The structure is the earliest known evidence of deliberate log-crafting to fit pieces together, and it predates the evolution of our own species. It was not made by Homo sapiens, and researchers cannot identify the maker for certain because no hominin remains were found with it. It was likely made by an earlier human relative

Researchers at RMIT University trained honeybees to identify the smaller of two numbers by rewarding them with a sweet sugar solution. When later presented with a completely blank image—a concept they had never seen before—the bees consistently chose it as being smaller than one, demonstrating an understanding of an empty set.

The International Space Station circles Earth roughly every 90–92 minutes at about 28,800 km/h, so its crew experiences around 16 sunrises and sunsets in 24 hours. NASA notes each sunrise or sunset lasts only a few seconds at that speed, turning the window view into a rapid-fire cycle of dawn and dusk.

In 1856, 18-year-old William Henry Perkin was trying to synthesize quinine, then used against malaria, when his failed coal-tar experiment produced a vivid purple residue. The result became mauveine, one of the first synthetic dyes, and helped open the door to the modern chemical industry.

Sacoglossan sea slugs pierce algae and keep the algae’s chloroplasts, the structures that perform photosynthesis, inside their own tissues. Recent research found those stolen chloroplasts can remain photosynthetically active for nearly a year in specialized compartments called kleptosomes.

The freshwater apple snail Pomacea canaliculata has camera-type eyes with structures comparable to human eyes, including a lens, retina and optic nerve. In a 2025 study, researchers completely removed the snail’s eye stalk and observed full regeneration of the eye bulb and stalk within about one month. That makes the species a rare living model for studying complex eye regeneration.

Researchers found that many chameleons have bony skull bumps beneath exceptionally thin skin, letting UV light reach the bone and re-emit as visible blue patterns. In some Calumma species, males have more of these fluorescent bumps than females, suggesting the glow may help with signaling or species recognition.

Bowhead whales are considered the longest-lived marine mammals, with scientists estimating that some individuals may reach 200-plus years. NOAA notes that stone harpoon tips found in harvested bowheads helped show they can live well over a century, while newer age-estimation methods point beyond 200 years.

The star-nosed mole’s 22 fleshy nose rays form a high-speed touch organ that helps it locate and handle prey in as little as 120 milliseconds.

Botanically, an avocado is a berry because it is a fleshy fruit with a single large seed, and its endocarp—the layer around the seed—is soft rather than stony. That makes it different from true stone fruits like peaches and cherries, even though its big central seed can make it look like one.

Four clay tablets in the Yale Babylonian Collection preserve the world’s oldest known culinary recipes. Three of the tablets date to around 1730 BCE, and their Akkadian cuneiform instructions include broths, meat stews and vegetable stews rather than sweet baked goods.

A pair of wool trousers found in China's Tarim Basin is about 3,000 years old and remains the oldest known example of pants. Their wide crotch, fitted legs and woven reinforcements point to a garment engineered for riding horses, not just covering legs.

During a Montana storm on January 28, 1887, witnesses described snowflakes "larger than milk-pans," with some measured at about 15 inches across and 8 inches thick. Guinness World Records still lists that report as the largest snowflake by dimensions.

International safety standards for children’s writing instruments specify ventilated pen caps so that, if a cap is accidentally inhaled, airflow is less likely to be completely blocked. That’s why many common ballpoint caps include a small hole: it’s a simple vent that can buy time until help arrives.

The company has said the name is a contraction of two Danish words — leg and god — chosen to match its mission. It’s a neat bit of branding that’s literally a built-in motto.

On April 12, 1961, Yuri Gagarin ate beef-and-liver paste from an aluminum tube during Vostok 1, then followed it with chocolate sauce the same way.

A 35mm motion-picture camera rode aboard V-2 rocket No. 13 after a launch from White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. From about 65 miles (105 km) up, it captured grainy black-and-white frames showing Earth against the darkness of space — years before satellites made space photography routine. The camera smashed on impact, but the film survived inside a protective steel cassette.

On a headland in A Coruña, the Tower of Hercules has served as a navigational lighthouse since Roman times, making it a rare piece of ancient infrastructure that still does its original job. The structure was substantially restored in the 18th century, but it preserves a Roman core and remains an active aid to navigation.

The "QR" stands for "quick response," reflecting the goal of being read faster and from more angles than traditional barcodes. What began as an industrial tracking tool quickly proved handy for everyday life — think tickets, coupons, restaurant menus, and more — because a phone camera can scan the same pattern.

Botanically, peanuts are edible seeds that grow in pods, which is why they’re classified as legumes rather than nuts. Harvard notes that despite the name, peanuts belong in the same broad plant group as soybeans and lentils.

On June 26, 1974, a Marsh Supermarket in Troy, Ohio, made checkout history when a 10-pack of Wrigley’s Juicy Fruit became the first item scanned with a Universal Product Code (UPC) barcode.

A single "megaflash" on Oct. 22, 2017, ran from eastern Texas to near Kansas City—about 515 miles (829 km). It wasn’t fully recognized until improved satellite reprocessing revealed the flash’s true, continuous extent.

That cloth-like "paper" is one reason a bill feels so different from printer paper. It also contains tiny red and blue fibers mixed throughout the bill as a built-in anti-counterfeiting feature.

In coin terminology, those little "grip lines" around the edge are a reeded edge, and the pattern itself is called reeding. The U.S. Mint even points out that dimes and quarters are reeded with little lines all around the edge, which is exactly what your finger feels when you roll one.

Barbie's real name Barbara" is a nod to Mattel co-founder Ruth Handler’s daughter, also named Barbara.

In 1957, NBS/NIST engineer Russell Kirsch used a rotating drum scanner and the SEAC computer to digitize a small photo of his infant son, Walden. The resulting file was just 176 pixels by 176 pixels — tiny by today's standards, but it helped kickstart modern computer imaging.

The word octothorpe is the dictionary term for the symbol # — the same mark people also call the hashtag, pound sign or number sign. So when you tap "#" on a phone keypad or type a hashtag online, you’re technically using an octothorpe.

Fredric J. Baur, the chemist credited with designing the original Pringles can, reportedly asked to have part of his cremated remains buried in one. After he died in 2008, his children put some of his ashes in an Original-flavor Pringles can and buried it with him; the rest were placed in urns.

That tiny dot over lowercase i's and j's is formally called a tittle in typography and dictionaries. It’s essentially a small dot/mark used as a diacritic.

Martin Waldseemüller’s 1507 wall map is often nicknamed "America’s Birth Certificate" because it’s the first known document where the name "America" appears. The name was printed on the map’s depiction of the newly described lands in the Western Hemisphere, helping the label catch on across European cartography.

Karel Čapek’s play R.U.R. (published in 1920) is credited with introducing the word "robot," drawn from the Czech term "robota" meaning forced labor. The play's first performance followed in 1921.

Deserts are defined by how little precipitation they get — not by heat or sand — so polar regions can qualify. National Geographic notes Antarctica is the largest desert on Earth at about 5.48 million square miles. Britannica likewise identifies the Antarctic Ice Sheet as the planet’s largest desert by area.

A Neolithic grave at Shillourokambos in Cyprus contained a human and a cat intentionally buried close together — about 40 cm (16 inches) apart. The finding predates clear Egyptian cat depictions by roughly 4,000 years, making it a standout early marker of the human–cat relationship.

In Ivanhoe, Scott uses "Free Lances" to mean hired soldiers whose loyalty isn’t tied to any one lord. The modern job sense kept the "works for whoever hires them" idea, just swapping battlefields for paychecks.

Guinness World Records certified the maze at "A Maze in Corn" in St. Adolphe, Manitoba, measuring it on Feb. 10, 2019. At 30,021 square feet, it’s a full-on winter labyrinth built from packed snow walls rather than hedges.

Big Ben’s replacement Great Bell cracked in 1859 after being struck with an overweight hammer, and instead of replacing it, workers altered the bell so the hammer would hit a different spot. The official historical account says they chipped out metal around the crack and turned the bell by one eighth of a turn; it has kept its slightly different tone ever since.

Phytoplankton perform photosynthesis just like plants on land, generating vast amounts of oxygen as a byproduct. Despite their microscopic size, their global abundance means they collectively produce roughly 50% of the oxygen in Earth’s atmosphere. This makes the oceans, not forests, the planet’s largest oxygen factory. Their health is critical, as changes in ocean temperature and chemistry can directly affect global oxygen production.

A single lightning bolt can heat the surrounding air to about 30,000 kelvin, roughly five times hotter than the sun’s surface. This causes the air to expand explosively, creating the shockwave we hear as thunder.

In April 1815, Mount Tambora in Indonesia erupted in one of the most powerful explosions in recorded history. The massive amounts of ash and sulfur dioxide ejected into the atmosphere blocked sunlight, causing global temperatures to drop in 1816.

Sweden’s "Dagen H" switch happened on September 3, 1967, when traffic changed from left-hand to right-hand driving, and the formal changeover resumed at 5:00 a.m. local time after vehicles had stopped and moved across shortly before that.

Long before texting, British Admiral John Arbuthnot Fisher used "O.M.G." in a letter dated September 9, 1917, addressed to Winston Churchill. The abbreviation was later noted by lexicographers as an early documented use of "OMG" meaning "oh my God."

France carried out its final guillotine execution on Sept. 10, 1977, when Hamida Djandoubi was executed in Marseille. Just months earlier, "Star Wars" premiered in theaters.

Austria-Hungary issued the first official postcards as a cheaper, faster alternative to letters, originally called "correspondence cards." They cost about half the price of a standard letter and required no envelope, making communication more accessible to the public. The idea quickly spread across Europe and beyond, shaping everyday communication long before email and texting.

In 1991, researchers at the University of Cambridge built a camera system to watch a coffee pot in their computer lab (the Trojan Room). The camera transmitted images over their local network. By 1993, it was connected to the internet, making it one of the first live online camera feeds, effectively the first webcam. The system ran for over a decade before being turned off in 2001.

On May 1, 1920, the Brooklyn Robins and Boston Braves played 26 innings—the most in MLB history—before the game was called due to darkness. Both starting pitchers, Leon Cadore and Joe Oeschger, threw all 26 innings themselves, allowing just one run each. Despite the marathon length, the entire game lasted only 3 hours and 50 minutes, far shorter than many modern games.

A note dated 12 June 1886 was sealed in a bottle thrown from the German sailing barque Paula during an ocean-current experiment. It resurfaced near Wedge Island, Western Australia, in January 2018, and the Western Australian Museum reported it as the world’s oldest known message in a bottle at the time. The find was authenticated by museum researchers working with German maritime and meteorological authorities.

In 1900, the Michelin brothers published a guide for motorists packed with practical travel info, including maps, fuel stops, restaurants and places to stay, because more road trips meant more tire wear and more tire sales. Eventually, the restaurant section of the Michelin guide had become so popular that the company started to recruit anonymous inspectors to visit and review restaurants. The star scale ranges from one star (a very good restaurant) to the coveted three stars (worth a special journey.)

Neptune hosts supersonic winds that can reach speeds over 1,200 mph (about 2,000 km/h). By comparison, Earth's peak winds only hit 250 mph (400 km/h.) Scientists believe these extreme winds are driven by internal heat escaping from the planet’s core rather than solar energy.

When a pistol shrimp snaps its oversized claw shut, it creates a cavitation bubble that collapses with a sharp pop, a shock wave and even a brief flash of light. NOAA says the snap can reach roughly 183 to 210 decibels, making these tiny crustaceans some of the loudest sound producers in the ocean.

Roman builders appear to have left tiny lime clasts in their concrete on purpose, and those particles could help seal cracks when water got in. In lab tests, researchers found that Roman-inspired concrete made with quicklime re-sealed fractures, helping explain why structures like Roman harbors, aqueducts, and domes have lasted so long.

The key molecule most associated with artificial banana flavor is isoamyl acetate (also called banana oil), and has been used as an odor-based test agent for respirators and gas masks. If the wearer could smell the banana-like odor, the mask fit or seal was inadequate. That use appears in U.S. fit-testing procedures and related safety guidance.

Male club-winged manakins produce a high, violin-like hum by rubbing specially adapted wing feathers together to court females. Researchers found the male can vibrate those feathers at more than 100 cycles per second, and its wing bones are unusually solid to help make the performance possible.

John Quincy Adams' daguerreotype is the earliest known surviving photo of a U.S. president. It was taken in March 1843, more than a decade after leaving the White House. That makes the image an overlap point between the founding generation and the brand-new technology of photography, which had been unveiled publicly only a few years earlier.

Sculptor Gutzon Borglum planned a grand "Hall of Records" inside Mount Rushmore to store key documents and explain the monument to future generations. The full chamber was never finished, but a tunnel remains behind Abraham Lincoln’s head, and a sealed repository with porcelain panels was later placed there.

Across 13th- and 14th-century European manuscripts, artists repeatedly tucked bizarre scenes of armored knights battling oversized snails into the margins. The image appears so often that it became one of medieval art’s strangest recurring visual jokes. Scholars still debate what it meant.

Researchers documented Atlantic puffins picking up small wooden sticks and rubbing them through their feathers, an example of a tool used for body care. The observation was notable because seabirds were not previously known for this kind of behavior. One sighting came in Wales and another in Iceland, suggesting the trick may not be a one-off accident.

The Ashmolean Museum opened to the public in 1683, making it Britain’s first public museum and the world’s first university museum. That means a visitor in Oxford today can walk into an institution that has been welcoming the public since the 17th century, long before the modern museum became a standard cultural fixture.

In normal lighting, the 45.52-carat Hope Diamond looks deep blue, but under ultraviolet (UV) light it emits a striking red phosphorescent afterglow. That "glow-in-the-dark" effect can linger even after the UV source is turned off, making it a rare optical signature of certain natural blue diamonds.

The famous hillside letters weren’t built to celebrate movies, but were put up to advertise an upscale housing development named Hollywoodland. Over time, the sign outgrew its sales pitch and became shorthand for the entire entertainment industry. In 1949, the "LAND" was removed during a refurbishment, leaving the iconic name recognized today.

Invented by the mathematician and engineer Hero of Alexandria, the machine was designed to prevent people from taking more holy water than they paid for in temples. When a coin was inserted into a slot, it fell onto a tray attached to a lever; the weight of the coin pulled the lever, opening a valve that let a set amount of water flow out. Once the coin slid off the tilting tray, the valve snapped shut, ending the transaction.

Photography enthusiast Robert Cornelius made a daguerreotype self-portrait in late 1839—long before cameras were pocket-sized. Because early exposures were slow, he reportedly had to sit motionless for about 10 to 15 minutes. The image is widely treated as an early (and often cited as the first) photographic "selfie."

Released in 1995, Toy Story wasn’t just Pixar’s debut feature—it was the first full-length movie produced entirely with computer animation, proving CGI could carry a whole story (not just special effects). That technical leap helped kick off the modern era of 3D animated features across Hollywood.

The earliest known printed use of "O.K." appeared on March 23, 1839, in the Boston Morning Post as a playful abbreviation for the intentionally misspelled phrase "oll korrect" ("all correct"). It grew out of a brief slang craze for humorous misspellings and abbreviations in the late 1830s. A year later, the term got an extra boost when it was echoed in U.S. political campaigning.

Only male platypuses can deliver venom, using a spur on each hind ankle that channels venom from a gland in the thigh. It’s not known for being deadly to humans, but documented stings can cause intense pain and swelling.

The hop between Westray and Papa Westray in Scotland’s Orkney Islands is widely cited as the world’s shortest scheduled flight. Orkney Islands Council and Guinness World Records note the route is 1.7 miles and can take less than a minute in the air.

In 1833, Abraham Lincoln partnered with his friend William F. Berry to open "Berry and Lincoln" in New Salem, Illinois, where they sold items like lard, sugar, and various spirits. While Lincoln eventually sold his interest in the business to pursue law and politics, his tavern license remains a notable artifact of his pre-presidential life.

"Flamboyance" is just one of a few collective nouns used for a gathering of flamingos. Other names include "stand" or "colony," but "flamboyance" is the memorable standout.

Even though its images feel far-flung, the Hubble Space Telescope is close enough to whip around Earth about 15 times a day. At that pace, it can see roughly 15 sunrises daily as it repeatedly crosses from night into day along its orbit.

In the 1820s, Joseph Nicéphore Niépce coated a polished pewter plate with bitumen of Judea (a naturally occurring asphalt) and placed it in a camera obscura to record a real-world scene. Light hardened the bitumen in brighter areas, and the softer, unexposed material was later washed away with solvents, leaving a permanent image on metal.

In 2019, researchers sequenced a complete ancient human genome from a 5,700-year-old lump of chewed birch pitch (which was used as chewing gum in the Stone Age) found at the Syltholm site on Lolland, Denmark. The Nature Communications paper reports approximately 2.3× genome coverage and also recovered the chewer’s oral microbiome and traces of recent foods. Genetic analysis showed the individual, nicknamed "Lola," was female and likely had dark skin, dark hair, and blue eyes.

The Louvre provides a small mailbox/mail slot for the "Mona Lisa," where visitors can leave letters (and flowers) addressed to the painting.

In the traditional Chinese lunisolar calendar, the new year starts on a specific new moon tied to the winter solstice, which is why it "floats" between late January and mid-February.

In 2023, researchers reported that a soil nematode (roundworm) from Siberian permafrost resumed activity after the surrounding material was radiocarbon-dated to roughly 46,000 years old. In the study, the worm belonged to a newly described species, Panagrolaimus kolymaensis, and survived via cryptobiosis—an extreme "pause" of metabolism.

Titan's lakes and seas are made of liquid hydrocarbons — mostly methane, with ethane — confirmed by NASA's Cassini radar measurements showing northern lakes and seas filled with methane and measuring hundreds of feet deep.

These receptors don’t create conscious taste, but instead act as chemosensors that help regulate local physiology. The receptors help regulate digestion, metabolism, and immune responses. In the airways, these receptors can even detect bacteria and trigger defensive reactions.

In 1984, the Seattle Seahawks became one of the first pro sports teams to retire the No. 12 jersey — not for a player, but for their fans, known as the 12s. This tribute celebrates how the crowd acts as a "12th player" by creating deafening noise and an intense home-field advantage at Seahawks games.

The Movile Cave system's entire food web is powered by bacteria that get their energy from oxidizing toxic gases like hydrogen sulfide instead of sunlight. These chemoautotrophic microbes fix carbon and form thick biofilms that feed dozens of eyeless invertebrate species, making Movile one of the very few known natural ecosystems whose productivity comes entirely from chemosynthesis rather than photosynthesis.

In experiments with wild American crows, researchers trapped birds while wearing a particular "dangerous" mask and later found that crows continued to single out and loudly scold that same face for at least 2.7 years, ignoring neutral faces nearby. Over time, more and more crows that were never trapped joined in, showing that they not only remember individual human faces but also socially spread the warning about which people to mob and avoid.

In 2021, scientists identified Brookesia nana, a chameleon so small that an adult male measures only 13.5 millimeters from snout to base of tail, roughly the length of a sunflower seed. Researchers confirmed the discovery through micro–CT scans that revealed fully developed reproductive organs, proving it was a mature adult despite its miniature size.

In 1964, Douglas Engelbart of the Stanford Research Institute developed the first prototype for a computer pointing device, which was housed in a carved block of North American cherry wood. The device featured two metal wheels on the bottom to track movement across a flat surface and a single red button on top. This primitive "X-Y Position Indicator for a Display System" laid the foundation for modern computing interfaces long before plastic became the industry standard.

Gallium, a silvery metal, melts at around 85.6 °F, and skin is around 89.6-95°F, so a small piece usually liquefies in a warm, closed palm. Education resources from the University of Waikato describe gallium as solid when you first pick it up but melting while it sits in your hand, then solidifying again when poured onto a cooler surface.

The Svalbard Global Seed Vault stores backup copies of crop seeds from gene banks worldwide in chambers reached by a tunnel running about 130 yards into a frozen mountain and cooled to –18°C. As of 2025 it holds just over 1.3 million seed samples from more than 6,000 plant species and 120+ countries, designed as an "insurance policy" so humanity can replant essential crops if war, disasters or climate change wipe out local collections.

A standard 52-card deck can be arranged in 52! different ways, which works out to about 8.07×10^67 possible orders. That number is so huge that any properly shuffled deck you hold is, for all practical purposes, a sequence of cards that has never appeared before in the entire history of card playing. In fact, 52! is roughly 10^17 times larger than the estimated number of atoms on Earth, so there still wouldn’t be enough atoms for each one to "stand in" for a different card ordering.

Researchers filmed a hadal snailfish (genus Pseudoliparis) at 8,336 meters in Japan’s Izu-Ogasawara Trench, the deepest fish observed to date.

On Nov. 30, 1954, a meteorite crashed through the roof of Ann Hodges' home near Sylacauga, Alabama, into the living room, bounced off a radio, and struck her while she napped on the couch, the first confirmed case of a meteorite hitting a person.

The term petrichor was coined in 1964 by Australian researchers to describe the earthy scent released when rain hits dry soil. The smell comes from plant oils and a molecule called geosmin, produced by soil-dwelling bacteria.

Researchers at Keio University trained pigeons to recognize the difference between Impressionist and Cubist styles. The birds were able to correctly identify paintings by Claude Monet and Pablo Picasso even when shown works they had never seen before.

This ability comes from hummingbirds' wing structure and powerful flight muscles, which let them rotate their wings in a figure-eight pattern to generate lift in multiple directions. Flying backward helps them feed efficiently on flowers and maneuver with precision among blossoms.

Researchers on Oʻahu found a newly described Hyposmocoma caterpillar that lives on spider webs and camouflages its silk case with body parts of trapped prey (e.g., ant heads, fly wings, spider legs). The grisly "bone collector" disguise likely helps it avoid the resident spiders while it scavenges or feeds.

The "Complaint tablet to Ea-nāṣir" is widely recognized as the oldest written customer-service complaint, dated to about 1750 BCE. It’s a clay tablet from Ur in which a buyer named Nanni berates a merchant named Ea-nāṣir for delivering inferior copper and mistreating his messenger.

Nichelle Nichols recounted that Martin Luther King Jr., a fan of Star Trek, personally urged her not to quit after Season 1, telling her the role of Uhura was too important for representation, so she withdrew her resignation and stayed.

While the Soviet dog Laika is often remembered as the first space traveler, a group of fruit flies actually reached the final frontier a decade earlier on Feb. 20, 1947. Launched by the United States aboard a captured German V-2 rocket, the insects were sent to an altitude of 67 miles specifically to study the biological effects of cosmic radiation at high altitudes. The mission was a success as the flies were recovered alive after their capsule safely parachuted back to Earth, proving that complex organisms could survive the journey.

Surgeons in the late 18th century developed a hand-cranked "chain saw" for symphysiotomy, a procedure to cut the pubic joint to widen the pelvis during obstructed labor.

Researchers discovered that the shape is formed within the final section of the intestine through uneven muscle contractions, which allow the corners of the waste to flatten into a cube.

From 1912 to 1948, the Olympics held art competitions including architecture, literature, music, painting and sculpture, with official gold, silver and bronze medals for works inspired by sport. They ended after a 1949 IOC decision that most entrants were professional artists, which clashed with the era’s amateurism rules.

French engineer Louis Réard named the bikini after Bikini Atoll in the Pacific, where the United States had just conducted highly publicized atomic bomb tests. Réard believed the swimsuit would create a similarly "explosive" cultural reaction.

The name "White House" emerged gradually in the 19th century and wasn’t made official until 1901, when President Theodore Roosevelt adopted it in formal documents.

Scientists have recovered around 48,000–50,000 meteorites from Antarctica.

After its dedication in October 1886, President Grover Cleveland ordered the Statue of Liberty placed under the U.S. Lighthouse Board; it went into lighthouse service on Nov. 22, 1886, and was maintained as an official aid to navigation. It was formally deactivated in 1902.

The Boomerang Nebula, about 5,000 light-years away, has a temperature of just 1 kelvin (–272.15 °C), making it colder than the cosmic microwave background. Astronomers discovered its extreme chill by studying how its expanding gas absorbs background radiation.

The moon is slowly drifting because of Earth’s rotation and the tides create a tug on the Moon, transferring energy that pushes it into a slightly higher orbit.

Axolotls can regenerate entire limbs and even repair parts of their heart, spinal cord and brain after injury, often restoring full function. In lab studies, scientists have watched amputated legs regrow, and internal tissues rebuild with minimal or no scarring.

This popular tradition started in the early 20th century when Spanish grape growers promoted it to sell more fruit. At the stroke of midnight on December 31, people race to eat one grape with each bell chime.

Through nuclear fusion, the Sun converts mass into energy, releasing it as light and heat. This process consumes roughly 4 million tons of solar material every second.

Koalas have ridged fingerprints so similar to humans that even high-resolution forensic analysis can struggle to tell them apart. Scientists believe this trait evolved independently in koalas as they adapted to gripping and manipulating eucalyptus branches.

After years of postal workers replying to Santa's mail on their own time, the U.S. Post Office Department officially launched what’s now called Operation Santa in 1912. articles.title: How the High Street became a window on our political instability
articles.summary: High Streets have declined in recent years. What does this tell us about the UK?
articles.body:
For a number of years, people around Britain have spoken of what they perceived to be "dodgy shops" on their High Street. To many, it seemed new businesses were popping up that had little obvious purpose or, in many cases, a huge number of direct competitors already in situ. Rumours spread between neighbours about money-laundering mini-marts and gang-owned vape stores.

There was a vague feeling of unease about all of this - but it was difficult for ordinary people living nearby to prove there was anything amiss.

And so when we started looking into the topic last February, I didn't truly appreciate the scale of what was really going on on our High Streets.

Our BBC team has travelled across the UK - including to Plymouth, Rochdale, Shrewsbury, Newport and Bradford - exposing what we have found to be brazen criminality on the High Street.

In Hull, we unearthed underground tunnels supplying sacks of illegal cigarettes to High Street mini-marts. In Swansea, we watched as officers smashed in windows of "stash cars" that were used to hide illegal cigarettes during the day, and deal drugs at night. And we exposed a network of high street shops selling illegal tobacco fronted by "ghost directors" masking the real owners.

Freedom of Information requests revealed for the first time that more than 3,600 shops across the UK had illegal goods - such as counterfeit cigarettes, tobaccos, and vapes - seized over 2024-25. The then-Home Secretary Yvette Cooper described some of our findings as a "disgrace". Throughout our reporting we were repeatedly attacked and threatened.

In lots of places, it seems, High Streets have become a front for organised crime. The National Crime Agency (NCA) estimates that at least £1bn of criminal cash is laundered through UK High Street stores each year.

"People want to feel safe… [going] down the local High Street," says John Herriman, chief executive of the Chartered Trading Standards Institute. "The concern is that they don't feel as safe as they used to."

Every episode of High Street criminality causes local angst. But when you look at the national picture - as we have done over the last year - another broader lesson emerges. High Streets seem to offer insight into Britain's troubles. Like a cracked mirror, they reflect other trends in British society, including lacklustre income growth, inequality and the boom in online shopping.

And some analysts tell us that obvious criminality on the High Street is shaping politics too, turning voters away from long-established parties and towards political newcomers.

So how did it get to this? And is there a solution for the decline of Britain's High Streets?

Organised crime has always existed on the High Street, says Elijah Glantz, a research fellow into organised crime at the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi), a security think tank.

"Nail bars, pubs, certain restaurants - anything that's cash-intensive has always been vulnerable to organised crime exploiting it," he says. Criminals like cash because unlike card transactions or bank transfers, it is largely untraceable, which makes it useful for both transactions and money laundering.

But in the last decade, he says, both the police and Trading Standards - a body enforcing consumer protection laws - have been squeezed. In 2002, there were 4,260 staff employed by Trading Standards, but in 2025 there were 2,378. Since then, crime has seemingly become more visible.

"There does seem to be an increase in the visibility of it. We're looking at organised crime that has manifested because nobody has put it away, nobody has forced it underground," says Glantz.

And that brazenness has a sharp psychological effect, analysts say - particularly on politics.

Nick Plumb, a director at the Power to Change think tank, says that the sight of open criminality on the High Street fuels feelings of "powerlessness" - a force that's proving potent in UK politics.

"The sense of a lack of control… has been a key feature of our politics over the last decade," he says. "High Streets are incredibly important [to] how people feel about the country… and politics."

And it's not just criminality that people care about. There is the issue of empty shops too.

In particular, Plumb's analysis showed that in the 2024 general election, support for Reform UK was higher in the 100 places in England with the biggest increases in persistent High Street vacancy relative to the rest of the country. This is based on parliamentary seats they won, or came second in. It built on previous research - from academics at the universities of Warwick and Oxford, and Imperial College London - that linked visible High Street decline to support for the United Kingdom Independence Party, an earlier political outfit of Nigel Farage, between 2009 and 2019.

Plumb says that "High Street decline is only partially explained by deprivation," and points to the "rise of online shopping and out-of-town retail, distant and uninterested ownership [and] changing working habits" as a factors behind the decline.

This decline often starts with those vacant units.

Glantz from Rusi thinks that as legitimate businesses close, crime moves in. "Rents are down, there's a lot of empty spaces, so landlords are willing to pretty much take just about anybody," he says.

Plumb came up with a new name for these areas: the "shuttered front", a string of constituencies with struggling High Streets that Power to Change think could play a pivotal role in future elections.

Indeed, Reform's Nigel Farage and Richard Tice were among the first mainstream politicians to regularly talk about visible signs of High Street criminality.

In 2024, Farage said at an event: "You can see High Streets with five, six, seven barber shops in them." Tice added: "Seriously, how come lots of these new barber shops have got no customers in them? How come they all want cash only? These are fronts for money laundering and drug money, and someone has to talk about it."

And in a social media video he made last year - one that quickly set parts of the internet alight - Robert Jenrick, who was then the shadow justice minister, listed "weird Turkish barber shops" as a visible sign of decline, alongside bike theft, phone theft, and drugs in town centres. "It's all chipping away at society," he said. He later clarified that he was "obviously not talking about all Turkish-style barber shops". Jenrick defected to Reform earlier this year.

Some politicians argue the language around High Street decline is in danger of becoming racially coded. In January, Miatta Fahnbulleh, then the devolution, faith and communities minister, agreed when asked by the Guardian if she thought the focus on Turkish barbers had racist overtones. "Yes, I do. The fundamentals aren't to do with the colour of the skin of people running our High Streets. It's to do with long-term decline and neglect."

At the time a Reform spokesman was quoted as saying: "This is not a matter of ethnicity.

"The National Crime Agency itself has said many of these establishments are used as fronts for money laundering as well as a whole range of criminality which is why they carried out hundreds of raids on them last year."

Meanwhile, immigration - the issue that voters consistently highlight as among the most pressing, and that Reform campaigns heavily on - came up in our investigation too. We exposed a Kurdish gang that was enabling migrants to work illegally in mini-marts the length of Britain, by offering to put their own names to official paperwork. Trading Standards told us they find a constant supply of staff from asylum hotels, who are vulnerable to abuse by employers, working in those shops.

Josh Nicholson, a researcher at the Centre for Social Justice think tank, says, "Chaos and flux in Westminster are reflected in our High Streets.

"People feel powerlessness, they look at Westminster and see an inability of politicians to grapple with the basics and that feeds down to a local level."

This feeling of helplessness came up again and again in our travels.

"Nothing is going to change," Daniel, in Swansea, told us about the criminality on his High Street, which has become a hub for counterfeit rolling tobacco. He has seen violence on the High Street and an increase in raids on High Street shops. He's a dual British and Chinese national and was considering moving to Hong Kong.

"It doesn't make me feel safe. I've got kids."

Oscar Selby, who researches troubled High Streets at the Centre for Cities think tank, sees them as a "bellwether" for the wider economy.

"High streets are ultimately… downstream of the broader economy's performance," he says. "The reason why people are so frustrated about High Streets is that people are also just annoyed that incomes have stagnated for the last 15 years. I think it all comes together in one package."

He thinks troubled High Streets are a "visual manifestation of the economic hardship that a lot of places feel".

High Street criminality sheds light on how bricks-and-mortar stores have been hammered by the boom in online shopping, with footfall 15-20% lower after the Covid lockdowns, according to a study from 2024. Amazon's net sales in the UK, however, have doubled since 2020. This has been exacerbated by the woes in the commercial property market, which was hit by the shift to working from home since lockdowns were introduced, and rising interest rates.

Of course, it's an uneven picture across the country. Some town centres appear to be thriving, and in those places you won't notice much visible sign of criminality - though the NCA did find organised High Street crime gangs in every part of the UK during an operation last year. Research from the Centre for Cities points to Cambridge, York, Edinburgh and Manchester as relative success stories. But this reflects another problem: inequality, because it tends to be places that are already wealthier that have less High Street crime. Towns that are already struggling, meanwhile, are the ones that attract money-laundering gangs.

Now, amid calls for Sir Keir Starmer's resignation, Westminster is paying more attention. Housing Secretary Steve Reed directly linked the state of High Streets to people's faith in politics.

"Each of the last four prime ministers have been the most unpopular ever and the reason for that is the public are very angry about the state of the economy, very angry about the state of our public services and very angry about what they see around them when they look at their High Streets and their hometown," Reed told the BBC.

The government has announced a new High Street organised crime unit, which will cost £30m over three years. About two-thirds of that will go towards the NCA, funding 75 officers. The rest will go to Trading Standards, with a small amount given to tax and immigration authorities.

The promise is that rogue barber shops, vape stores, mini-marts and sweet shops will face thousands of raids.

Glantz from Rusi thinks the extra cash will make some difference, and hopes the new officers hired at the NCA will spend time looking in detail through company documents and help to "peel back the layers of ownership structures, which is very difficult to do".

He adds: "If you get specialist investigators at the NCA to look, you will get a better threat picture and start to understand who is at the end of it."

But he doesn't think £30m over three years is enough to make up for long-term cuts to police and Trading Standards budgets - though he does say that a small number of flashy, highly visible raids on shops, if shared widely on social media, could have a deterrent effect.

"There hasn't been that visible community policing that might have in the past deterred these very obvious shops from springing up."

To take truly tough action, Glantz says, authorities need extra powers.

Currently, if Trading Standards want to shut a business, they usually have to use anti-social behaviour powers. But it requires lots of paperwork, and it's a tough bar to meet: it must be proved that a business is a serious nuisance, or that disorderly, offensive or criminal behaviour is likely to occur.

On the few occasions when Trading Standards can shut a business permanently, it's generally by working with landlords, who evict tenants.

Instead, Trading Standards wants stronger, direct powers to close illegal shops quickly, and to shut down crime networks operating in multiple premises across High Streets (to end the whack-a-mole strategy where criminals simply shift their illegal goods to another shop they own next door).

Partly in response to the BBC's journalism, the government has now ordered a "rapid review" of local responders' powers; in particular, it will look at whether Trading Standards should be able to close a potentially criminal shop for longer than the initial three months.

Herriman, from the Chartered Trading Standards Institute, thinks that for too long High Street organised crime was seen as a local problem rather than a national one, in part because Trading Standards activities are devolved to councils.

"Actually what it needs is some strategic direction from [national] government… because then you can start to coordinate across the country," he says.

The newly announced cash, Herriman says "is not job done, it is just job started".

Perhaps the biggest lesson from our year-long investigation was this: people still fundamentally care about their High Streets.

In the 1990s, it was out-of-town shopping centres that were predicted to kill off High Streets; then it was online shopping, then working from home.

But travelling the country, we found that High Streets still occupy a special place in our psyche. That's why the sight of brazen criminality causes such distress.

One pensioner in Oldham urged us to keep going, because "nobody cared". Richard, in north-west London, asked us in desperation for tips to investigate gangs himself. And I'll never forget Errol, a Kurd from Turkey who had spent decades building his grocer's shop in Pill, south Wales. He said he could no longer compete with gangs, and was tempted to give up and leave. He stayed mostly for his children and grandchildren, who were born in Britain.

Now, it's the task of the government and police to fix it.

articles.title: Resident doctors in England call off strike after new offer from government
articles.summary: The walkout had been due to start at 07:00 BST on Monday and last until Friday.
articles.body:
Resident doctors in England have called off strikes which were scheduled to begin on Monday.

The British Medical Association (BMA) said the government had "made a new offer" at the last minute which would be put to its members for a vote.

The walkout had been due to run from 07:00 BST on Monday 15 June until 06:59 Friday 19 June. It would have been the 16th in the long-running dispute over pay.

Health Secretary James Murray said the new offer was a "chance to draw a line under the damaging disputes of recent years" while the BMA said it had held up its "end of the bargain" after the government shifted its position.

The two sides had been in talks for days - including on Saturday, just hours before the strike was called off.

It came too late to avoid some patient disruption over the coming week.

While NHS England said 95% of operations and appointments were due to go ahead, thousands have been postponed. Reinstating them on the original timetable will be a tough task for hospitals.

Government sources said there was no extra money on the table for this year - but that the offer proposed faster increases next year in pay scales.

In addition, it promised 4,500 extra training places for newly qualified doctors and that doctors' exam fees would be covered.

Previously known as junior doctors, resident doctors have received pay rises worth 33% over the past four years, including a 3.5% increase this year.

It means starting salaries are now just over £40,000, with the most senior resident doctors getting £76,500 in basic pay. They can earn thousands more each year for things like working unsociable times and additional hours.

But the BMA argues they are still being paid a fifth less than they were in 2008 once inflation is taken into account.

Health Secretary James Murray said: "It is a positive and welcome development - especially for patients - that the BMA have called off these unnecessary strikes."

"The country simply cannot afford to increase the pay offer for this year. I am pleased that the BMA have recognised this, which has allowed us to make progress in other areas, such as training places and working conditions."

Dr Jack Fletcher, chairman of the BMA's resident doctors committee, said: "We have always been clear that no strikes needed to go ahead if we received an offer appropriate to put to our members.

"This should not have been left to the last moment, but we hold up our end of the bargain when the government shifts its position."

Sir Ciarán Devane, chief executive of the NHS Alliance, called the strike's suspension a "vital chance to reset the conversation" and urged both sides to strike a "fair, sustainable agreement".

It is understood the strike was originally called after Murray made it clear during a meeting in May that he was not willing to negotiate on pay, saying the union's demands were "unrealistic and unaffordable".

The BMA said he had showed "the same unwillingness to move" as his predecessor, the former health secretary Wes Streeting.

The union has called a series of strikes in England over pay and working conditions since 2023.

The most recent was a six-day walkout in April, after the BMA rejected an offer which included more training jobs, faster career progression and a plan to cover out-of-pocket expenses like exam fees.

articles.title: UK starts first vaccine trial, eight weeks into Ebola emergency
articles.summary: The UK medicines regulator has given approval for an experimental vaccine to be tested on healthy adults.
articles.body:
A new vaccine to tackle Ebola will now be tested on people after the UK regulator gave permission for trials to take place.

Scientists at the University of Oxford started developing the vaccine eight weeks ago when a public health emergency was declared on 17 May.

It is the first - out of four vaccines under development - to enter clinical trials.

Volunteers are being recruited, with the first doses expected to be given to healthy adults in the UK "within weeks".

The Ebola epidemic, centred on the Democratic Republic of the Congo has killed 625 people with 1,792 laboratory confirmed cases.

It is caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which has started two outbreaks before.

The six different species of Ebola are known as "sisters rather than twins" because while they are similar, they need separate treatments and vaccines. It means there are no approved drugs or vaccines this time.

The outbreak is still not under control and is taking place in a conflict zone with very mobile populations – heightening the need for a vaccine to help stop the spread of disease.

Dr Katrina Pollock, the chief investigator of the trial based at the University of Oxford, told the BBC: "We're doing phase one (early stage) trials of new vaccines all of the time, precisely to be ready for exactly this kind of outbreak."

The trial will be on 50 healthy adults aged 18-55. Researchers are also working with partners in Uganda to prepare for trials in Africa.

Volunteers will be monitored for a year, but scientists should know quickly whether the vaccine is producing the right kind of immune response or any unexpected side effects.

The Oxford team have been able to develop their vaccine in a matter of weeks because they are using the same technology that shot to fame during the Covid pandemic and was used in the Oxford/AstraZeneca Covid vaccine.

It uses a common cold virus that infects chimpanzees that has been genetically modified to make it safe.

This acts like an envelope and all the researchers need to do is change the letter inside before posting it into the body.

In Covid, the letter being delivered was a snippet of genetic code from the Covid virus.

This time it's a snippet from the Bundibugyo species of Ebola.

The vaccine does not cause an infection, but the piece of the genetic code starts producing one viral protein from Ebola inside the body.

This is enough to trigger the immune system to recognise a threat and mount an immune response.

That means the body should already have a head start if it encounters Ebolavirus for real.

The vaccine has been developed, tested on mice and macaque monkeys, and is being manufactured to a clinical standard by the Serum Institute of India. It has manufactured and stockpiled around 620,000 doses.

Based on that data, the UK's Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency has given the go-ahead for human trials.

Vaccine researcher Alex Sampson told the BBC: "As soon as we heard there was an outbreak, we were able to scale up really, really quickly."

Vaccines can normally take up to a decade to research, develop and prove effective. But Sampson says no corners are being cut.

"We're doing all the same tests that we would normally do, just we're able to do them in parallel, so it means a lot of teams working in lots of different places around the clock, but we're still doing everything that we would normally," he added.

What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult?

The Oxford Covid vaccine was estimated to have saved six million lives in the first year it was used around the world and hundreds of millions of doses have been taken.

However, the vaccine was also restricted for use in some countries because of rare blood clots which affected up to one in 100,000 people.

It is possible this vaccine carries the same risk, although this is much lower than the threat from the Bundibugyo species of Ebola which kills around a third of those infected.

Pollock said severe side effects are "very rare" and they thought "very deeply" about the implications for trials on healthy people, and that any risk would be communicated to volunteers.

"I want to stress that the Covid AstraZeneca vaccine was given to millions of people safely," she added.

There are three other vaccines being developed for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola.

These include one from biotechnology company Moderna using their mRNA vaccine technology. The International Aids Vaccine Initiative and Public Health Vaccines, based out of the US, are using the same technique that has been proven to work for another species of Ebola, but is slower to manufacture.

articles.title: Sarwar ministerial role sees promotion of another Starmer critic
articles.summary: Months after calling on Keir Starmer to quit, the Scottish Labour leader is set to become a minister in Burnham's government, the BBC's political editor writes.
articles.body:
The imminent appointment of the Scottish Labour leader Anas Sarwar to Andy Burnham's government, via a seat in the House of Lords, sees the promotion of another key figure in the downfall of Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister.

When Sarwar said publicly, back in February, that Sir Keir should stand down, it was a moment of colossal jeopardy for the now former prime minister.

It looked, briefly, like it might bring about an immediate and irrevocable collapse in his authority. Then, one after another, cabinet ministers posted their support for him on social media.

As I wrote at the time , missives of public loyalty from cabinet ministers towards a prime minister shouldn't be newsworthy and they only become so when the opposite seems feasible.

Now, five months on, Sarwar will be swapping Holyrood for Westminster and becoming a minister.

He will be joining Miatta Fahnbulleh in government, the new energy secretary in Burnham's cabinet, who was the first government minister to resign from Sir Keir's administration saying she had lost faith in him .

Also around the cabinet table, the new Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who let it be known in what turned out to be Sir Keir's final weeks in office that he had suggested to him that he ought to accept that his time was up.

It is also worth mentioning too John Healey, who resigned as defence secretary, and Wes Streeting, who resigned as health secretary towards the end of Sir Keir's time in Downing Street, are now in prominent roles in Burnham's cabinet as chancellor and defence secretary respectively.

This is the backdrop to comments from Steve Reed, the former communities secretary and doughty defender of Sir Keir at some of his moments of most intense peril.

Reed wrote to Burnham as he left government and said: "I hope those who did not show loyalty to Keir will now show it to you. I am proud that I acted with integrity at every step over the turbulent past few months."

There is, right now, as you would expect, overwhelming support for Burnham among Labour MPs.

But these public remarks from Reed are an indicator of the wells of private hurt and anger created by the events of recent days, weeks and months.

It is a reminder that, of course, all the folk you are reading and hearing about are human beings who have each keenly felt the tremors of uncertainty in recent months – and depending on their circumstances, outlook, instincts and judgement, have arrived at differing conclusions and decisions about how to act.

The public intervention of Darren Jones, another loyal lieutenant of the former prime minister, taking a swipe at the funding of the government's planned cut in VAT on domestic electricity bills should be seen in this context too.

Labour's switch from one leader to another was less drawn out and dramatic than it might have been, as there was neither a formal leadership challenge to Sir Keir, nor more than one contender to replace him once he had announced his intention to go.

But it is also true that what we have witnessed the climax of this week, and the build up to for months on end, is not cost or pain free for a political party and some of that is manifesting itself now – and may still do for some time.

articles.title: Chris Mason: What his first week in power tells us about Andy Burnham
articles.summary: The fledgling Burnham administration has been seeking to find its feet and make a decent first impression at the same time, the BBC's political editor Chris Mason explains.
articles.body:
"We are on borrowed time if we don't get a move on," Angela Rayner, the former deputy prime minister who is back in the cabinet this week as housing secretary, told the BBC's Today programme on Friday.

It has been quite the week at Westminster. Sir Keir Starmer's departure as prime minister on Monday seems rather a while ago.

The fledgling Burnham administration has been seeking to find its feet and make a decent first impression at the same time, as many try to do in the first days in a job.

There has been an early pattern in these early days: an early morning nugget of news dropping from No10.

On Thursday, it was business rates in England ; on Wednesday, it was bus fares in England and on Tuesday, it was a VAT cut on electricity bills .

Today, the prime minister is assembling what Rayner calls "a pride of mayors" among others for a meeting of what is known as the National Economic Council at the new No 10 North in Manchester.

Andy Burnham claims his new base in Manchester represents the beginning of " the biggest rebalancing of power our country has seen " and he will be "bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years".

His early announcements have been considerably more piecemeal than that – he says his "10 year plan for Britain" will come later in the year.

It is worth remembering there was talk from both Boris Johnson and his allies and from Sir Keir Starmer about their plans for the decade ahead – both fizzled out rather more quickly than that.

So how should we assess how much politics has changed, or not?

The early evidence - and let's be frank, it is only that given we are just a few days in - points to Andy Burnham being both more sharp and more nimble than his predecessor in setting out what he is attempting to do and trying to point to early examples of what that might look like, with the announcements of the last few days.

With the tinkering of how the government is run, like the creation of the Office of Prime Minister, and the establishment of No 10 North, he's made it clear that the arteries of power flow very much to and from him.

He hopes he can overcome the critique of Sir Keir Starmer and others, that one of the frustrations of being prime minister can be pulling levers and nothing actually happens.

Burnham's opponents are having to recalibrate and work through how they take on a new prime minister.

The Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's al fresco speech and news conference on a rooftop in central London on Thursday was a tacit acknowledgement that the political terms of trade have changed.

She teased the new prime minister over his informal style – he "seems like a nice guy…I'm glad he's got a sense of humour," she told us, before getting to the essence of her critique, that his offer was superficial, and thin.

"Is that it?" she asked, adding: "He is behaving like he's still the mayor of Manchester. He is now the prime minister of the United Kingdom."

Burnham wants to project a sense that he gets it - the cost of living pressures so many feel so acutely - and he is getting a move on.

But in just these first few days there has been a reminder that life comes at you fast as prime minister.

Firstly, on the domestic front – his intervention on the early release of prisoners in England and Wales, demanding what he calls a "pause", is a case study in the dilemmas of governing: crowded prisons and, so, difficult choices between least worst options – which criminals to free first.

Secondly, on the international front – after Burnham renewed America's permission to use British airbases for what are called "defensive" strikes on Iran, Tehran is claiming those bases are now legitimate targets. And, with the conflict in the Middle East escalating, the oil price is spiking again .

Then there are the huge questions that tumble from Burnham's big promises.

He has pledged, for instance, "the biggest council house building programme since the post war period." How would this be paid for? And what does the promise actually mean?

It is worth a listen to Matt Chorley's interview with Angela Rayner on BBC Radio 5 Live on precisely this point - the housing secretary isn't able to define when the "post war period" ended and therefore there is no numerical target attached to what appears to be a rather bold promise.

And this on the same day that Rayner acknowledging keeping Labour's promise to build 1.5 million new homes in England by 2029 looks rather shaky: she told the BBC it was "a difficult target".

What about defence spending? The new chancellor, John Healey, packed it in as defence secretary because he thought the department he now runs, the Treasury, didn't get it when it came to keeping us safe.

Let's see how he gets on now the boot is on the other foot.

Burnham is cutting business rates for some in England, but what of Labour's promise in its manifesto two years ago to "replace the business rates system, so we can raise the same revenue but in a fairer way." Will that happen?

And beyond the symbolism of having a prime ministerial office outside London, what, in practical terms, can No10 North actually achieve? How much clout and authority is it given? Just how often will senior ministers be there? And how much will it cost?

Civil servants are being asked if they would like to relocate to the north west of England. The indications from Team Burnham is they take it hugely seriously, but does the civil service truly respond to that, and given the turbulence in politics in recent years, is it an idea that lives beyond this prime minister?

Given the intended long term home of No 10 North is currently a building site and is not due to be finished until 2032 , this is a live question.

Sackings, cabinet surprises and policies: Burnham's first 24 hours as PM

Senior ministers and aides set to work from No 10 North

Burnham has big ideas - but what will they cost?

And how many noises off do we hear from grumpy Starmerites as the early novelty of governing dilutes? Given the speed with which one, Darren Jones, went public with a grumble it will be something Team Burnham will be wary of.

Then, there is the new prime minister's boldest claim of all – that he will be "bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years". Really? He describes a desire for a "new political model and a new economic model".

It is an understatement to say this triggers a cascade of questions. Including, for some of his critics, including Reform UK, a key one – where is your mandate for doing this?

The fascinating question of the coming months is the extent to which Andy Burnham can credibly or not, as voters see it, set a pathway towards the change he wants and then, in time, call a general election asking for an endorsement of his ideas and direction.

It is three years until there has to be an election, but the timing up until then is in his gift.

His opponents are publicly saying bring it on when there is talk of an election sooner rather than later. Privately, plenty of Conservative and Reform folk acknowledge they are not ready yet.

Could Andy Burnham be tempted? When asked, he has said "we're in a parliamentary democracy and, as we've seen through time, if somebody can command a majority of the MPs in the House of Commons, they obviously then have the legitimacy to lead things forward." That is a statement of constitutional truth, rather than a definitive answer either way to the question itself.

Many prime ministers arriving in office between general elections crave their own mandate. Gordon Brown reflects in his memoirs the agonising private conversations he had about a snap election and in deciding against it found himself going "from near hero to near zero in a day."

Boris Johnson went for it in 2019 and got a near-landslide out of it.

Theresa May, on the other hand, went for it in 2017 and ended up losing the majority she had inherited. The recent history books, then, offer a less than clear guide and Burnham has inherited a colossal majority.

His decision and its timing will likely be driven by how quickly and how much he can do with it.

In other words, whether he is popular enough.

articles.title: HMP Erlestoke prisoners using art as part of rehabilitation
articles.summary: Inmates say it is "rewarding" to create artwork and sell it online with the help of a charity.
articles.body:
A charity is supporting the rehabilitation of prisoners by offering them the opportunity to create and sell their own artwork.

Prisoners at HMP Erlestoke, in Wiltshire, have created their own artwork as part of the Prison Art Project scheme which is supported by homeless charity ALABARÉ. Participants are able to sell their work online with 50% of the proceeds going to the artist.

Many of the participants said creativity helped with their mental health and wellbeing while others said it felt "rewarding" to produce artwork.

Laura Joy, from the charity, said: "Artwork really gives people a chance to do meaningful activity towards rehabilitation and to support better choices."

Participants are provided with an art pack full of supplies like acrylics, pencils, watercolours and pastels with the condition that they create up to four pieces of artwork.

If their work is purchased, the artist receives half of the profits with the remainder used to fund the purchase of materials for others on the scheme.

Travellers' site shooting victim is named

The project has had more than 3,000 participants since it began in the 1960s.

There are currently 100 artists participating from 37 prisons and young offender institutions across England and Wales and more than 1,500 pieces of art were waiting to be uploaded and sold online.

Joy said the scheme was "a way of giving back" and a way to give the artists a "huge sense of pride".

She said: "We know how underfunded and overcrowded prisons are and there are not opportunities in some prisons for the people in prison to study art.

"I'm delighted that participants are having their artwork seen outside of their cells and internal art classes.

"Many of the pieces have some incredible personal stories behind them and capture a world view that is often hidden."

articles.title: National Trust expands park by 32 hectares in Saltram
articles.summary: Former agricultural land is turned into a public park in Plymouth, the National Trust says.
articles.body:
Former agricultural land has been turned into additional public park space for people in Plymouth, the National Trust has said.

The 32 hectares (79 acres) of green space has "significantly" increased the size of the trust's land in Saltram and included a new 2.5km (1.5 mile) multi-use trail suitable for all users funded by Sport England through the National Lottery and the Trust, it said.

It added a series of rest stops had also been installed along the trail, offering "stunning views across Plymouth" and linking with Saltram's existing paths including The Dell.

National Trust Saltram general manager Jez McDermott said the opening was "a landmark moment" for Plymouth and Saltram.

He said: "This investment in access, wellbeing and nature means more people can enjoy everything Saltram has to offer.

"Whether you're walking, wheeling, cycling, spending time with family or simply taking a moment to enjoy the views, we hope Saltram East becomes a place that people return to for generations to come."

The trust said investments had been made to "boost the diversity" of nature and wildlife in the area and that it had planted new wildflower hay meadows across the site to create homes for wildlife.

It said it also planned to create a community forest by planting up to 12,000 trees in the coming winter.

The trust said the existing country park attracted about one million visits each year and it expected the additional land to provide "significant health and wellbeing benefits" for locals.

Lisa Dodd-Mayne, of Sport England, said access to nature "shouldn't be a luxury".

She said: "In a growing city like Plymouth, these new trails will make it easier for more people to build active travel into everyday life, get outdoors and enjoy the health and wellbeing benefits of green spaces close to home."

articles.title: Argos is getting a makeover - but can it attract new shoppers?
articles.summary: The retailer has been around for 50 years but struggled to compete with newer rivals such as Amazon. Can its new owners turn it around?
articles.body:
Do you still shop at Argos? And if so, what do you think of it?

The chain has been a fixture of the British High Street for more than 50 years and is still used by around half of all UK households.

But it has struggled to thrive in recent years amid fierce competition from online giants like Amazon, with sales stagnating.

Its owner Sainsbury's recently announced it was selling the chain for a lot less than it paid for it just 10 years ago.

But the new owners say they see "real opportunities" for growth, including opening new standalone shops. Can they succeed where Sainsbury's did not?

When the BBC spoke to shoppers in central London this week, the retailer seemed to divide opinion.

Some, like Enrico, 28, said they loved the convenience of same-day collection, and felt nostalgic towards a brand which unlocked fond childhood memories.

"It was a great way of doing your Christmas shopping," he told the BBC. "We'd go into our local Argos and we'd get the massive print catalogue."

Argos's encyclopedia-like catalogue was once dubbed "the laminated book of dreams", but the company stopped printing it in 2021 .

At one point it was Europe's most widely printed publication.

For others, though, Argos has not moved with the times and is at odds with the seemingly endless online choice.

"I feel Amazon is a lot easier because it gets delivered straight to your door with Prime," said Emily, 22, adding that she only used Argos to buy appliances, not "day to day" items.

Jack Cunningham, 26, from Kent often uses Argos to pick up things when he's at work in London.

The scientist said the big draw was convenience: "If I need something in the moment and can't wait for delivery, normally I'll get it in Argos.

"You can order something really cheap on Amazon, and it might come and be the wrong size, " he added.

For years, commentators have asked whether Argos could build a business to take on Amazon, the biggest online seller in the UK.

But while Argos has invested a lot in digital, it never quite happened. It made £4.1bn of sales last year, compared with £32bn for Amazon in the UK.

Argos does, however, offer something its online rivals don't - a large network of stores, concessions in Sainsbury's shops, and collection points that mean customers can click and collect on the same day, free of charge.

Retail analyst Catherine Shuttleworth thinks Argos could capitalise on this, along with its reputation as a trusted British brand.

However, she thinks it needs to improve its app so it can compete with online players like Amazon, Shein and Temu.

"I think if you asked people to name five High Street retailers, they wouldn't name Argos," she added. "It's almost about reminding people it exists."

Argos hasn't been front of mind for Georgia, 27, for ages. She thinks it is outdated and not for her. "It's very old school isn't it? I'm more of an Amazon shopper."

Argos could also do better on customer service, thinks Hugh Radojev, editor of Retail Week.

"It's not an exciting place to shop, or what it used to be for kids around Christmas. Under a new ownership you'd hope they could get it back into the zeitgeist."

Since 2012, Argos has gone from having 845 standalone shops to around 200 - although it also has opened about 450 shop-within-shops in Sainsbury's stores.

This was seen as a smart move, allowing Argos to tap into Sainsbury's large customer base. Argos will keep all of those concessions after the takeover, and customers will continue to get Nectar loyalty card points for all their purchases.

But Nicole, 40, an Argos fan from South London, says she wants the chain to expand further.

"It would be nice if they could go in other supermarkets like Tesco," she added.

'Argos has a history of being different'

Argos's new owners have ruled out deals with rival supermarkets, but they do plan to forge other "partnerships" and open new standalone stores.

The group, called Swift Partners, includes several seasoned retail veterans, one of them a former boss of Co-operative Group. Retail analyst Richard Hyman thinks this ownership will be a better fit than Sainsbury's, which was focused on selling food.

But he is sceptical about how much Argos can grow in such a "tough retail market".

Shuttleworth is more optimistic, saying with a "ruthless focus" Argos can thrive and even put Amazon under pressure.

"Argos completely revolutionised the way we shop when they came out and they have a history of being different," she said. "If I was marketing director I would be thinking about how to bottle that for 2027."
