articles.title: The ultimate dog-friendly road trip on Minnesota's North Shore from Duluth to Grand Marais
articles.summary: From Split Rock Lighthouse to Pincushion Mountain, a dog-friendly road trip reveals why Minnesota's North Shore demands more than three days.
articles.body: A few weeks ago, I set out with the intention of writing an itinerary for the ultimate dog-friendly vacation on the Minnesota North Shore. Turns out, that's not as easy as I thought. Not for a lack of writing material, either. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS No, the challenge I ran into was that I couldn't fit all the outdoor adventures the area had to offer into the measly three days I planned to visit. Not a bad problem to have. Every summer, my husband and I visit my mother-in-law at her snowbird summer home in Minocqua, Wisc. During that trip, we like to take a few days to drive up to Lake Superior and see what kind of hiking we can find. In 2024, we explored the Porcupine Mountains in Michigan's Upper Peninsula. Last year, it was the Apostle Islands at the tippy top of Wisconsin. YOU DON'T NEED A KAYAK TO APPRECIATE NORTHERN WISCONSIN'S APOSTLE ISLANDS This year, we figured we'd try Minnesota. So I booked us a little Airbnb right on the lakeshore in Tofte, we threw our packs, our boots and our German Shepherd in the truck, and away we went. Day 1: Iona's Beach & Split Rock Lighthouse Admittedly, before this trip, I knew nothing about the stretch of land between Duluth and the Canadian border — aside from the fact that it's very cold in the wintertime, and I imagined every guy up there probably looked something like the Brawny Man. So I relied on my old friend Google (and my very helpful Nightcaps readers) to build our itinerary. Did you know there are eight state parks in that 150 miles of shoreline? EIGHT. So I knew we, sadly, weren't going to hit them all on this trip. We'd have to pick a few and save the rest for next year. At least a couple dozen people told me I had to go to Betty's Pies in Two Harbors — an iconic little café that's been around for 70 years. They have, I'm told, the best pies in all of Minnesota. Maybe all the Midwest. And like an idiot, I didn't listen. Instead, our first stop was at Iona's Beach. Which was delightful, too. Iona's Beach is a cute little crescent-shaped shore in Two Harbors that, instead of sand, is covered by salmon-colored pink rocks. In other words, this is not the sort of beach where you stroll barefoot. The stones are pink because they're made of rhyolite, a rock formed from ancient volcanic activity. The area is named after a sweet little old lady named Iona Lind, whose family originally owned the land and ran the resort that used to stand where the parking lot is now. Supposedly, the pebbles make a "singing" sound as Lake Superior's waves shift them back and forth against each other. But if I'm being honest, they just sounded like regular rocks to me. Still, Iona's Beach is worth your time for a quick stroll and some photos along the shore. Next up, we hit Split Rock Lighthouse. A couple of things to note about Split Rock Lighthouse: After hitting the Tofte General Store beer-bait-barbecue-and-tackle shop (not what it's called, but it should be) for some food to cook, we headed to our Airbnb. Friends, when I tell you it was like stepping back in time, I mean it. This particular property was built in the early 1970s and almost certainly has not been updated since. Our particular condo, though, had a 90s vibe — complete with an impressive collection of VHS tapes. We're talking "Liar Liar," "A Few Good Men," "Forrest Gump," "Titanic"! All the hits. But we didn't choose this rental for the decor. We chose it because it's located smack on the top of a cliff overlooking Lake Superior. The kind of view that makes you want to pop open a bottle of wine, sit down in an Adirondack chair and just stare into the horizon. And you best believe that's what I did. Day 2: Palisade Head & Tettegouche State Park We planned Wednesday to be our big hiking day. But first, a quick stop to check out the giant rock formation they call Palisade Head. It's a 300-foot granite cliff created in the Ice Age, and it's a seriously cool challenge for rock climbers. Or you can take the easier route like we did. Park your car in the designated viewing area and admire Palisade Head from afar. While we were there, we made conversation with a couple of dudes who proceeded to list all the cool hiking spots we needed to check out during our trip to the North Shore. It was at this moment I realized I should have scheduled out more than three days. HERE’S HOW TO DO THE SMOKY MOUNTAINS WITHOUT TRAFFIC AND CROWDS From there we headed to Tettegouche State Park. I kept pronouncing it "Tet-uh-GOOCH-ee" (à la "way down yonder on the Chattahoochee.") However, a sign in the visitor center informed me the correct pronunciation is "TET-uh-goosh." Bummer. There are roughly 23 miles of hiking trails in Tettegouche, so we hopped on AllTrails and created our own adventure: Shovel Point to High Falls to Two Step Falls. I think we made the right choice. Our route took us out to the lake shore, down along the river, to an incredible swimming hole at the base of High Falls, through some woody terrain and into a peaceful little lunch spot on the stream at Two Step. It worked out to about 6.2 moderate miles with multiple spots for Rocky to hop in the water and cool off. High Falls was the star of the show. On our way back to the condo, we decided to drive up Oberg Mountain. The loop gave us stunning vistas and a really cool overlook of Oberg Lake. I was pretty tired after Tettegouche, but this was well worth the extra 2.5 miles. That night we headed up to Moguls Grill & Taproom for post-hike burgers and beers. It's inside the Caribou Highlands Lodge, which serves as a ski resort in the wintertime. Dogs aren't allowed inside the restaurant, but we snagged some food to go and sat out on the patio. There, we met a nice elderly lady named Patrice who said she comes to the North Shore a few times a year "to escape the far-left hell scape of Minneapolis." Day 3: Pincushion Mountain, Grand Marais & Cascade River State Park Those fellas up on Palisade Head told us we have to check out the Gunflint Trail. So much great hiking on the Gunflint Trail! Beautiful country! Such cool wildlife! I see moose all the time! I do not love the idea of running into a grumpy moose out on the trail. But their sales pitch got me. Upon further research, though, I discovered the Gunflint Trail is actually a 57-mile byway that stretches all the way from the lakeshore into the Boundary Waters and damn near to Canada. Since we didn't budget enough time to cover all that ground, we chose the very first trail off the Gunflint: Pincushion Mountain. On the way up US 61, though, we stopped at a local coffee shop called Fika that came highly recommended by our Airbnb host. Holy cow, you guys, are you familiar with maple syrup lattes? Because they are, I learned, very much a thing in northern Minnesota. Now listen, I drink my coffee like my grandpa does: strong, black and by the bucket. One step short of jet fuel. But what's the point of driving 16 hours from home if you don't try the local fare? My goodness. That maple syrup latte was worth every bit of the (probably) 500 calories it cost me. What a concept. Consider it fuel for the 5.75-mile Pincushion Mountain Loop. Half of this trail was on an old logging road, which the curmudgeonly reviewers on AllTrails didn't love. I swear people on AllTrails will complain about everything. The grass was too tall in some places. I had to step over a log. A bug landed on my shoulder! You're in the woods, Sharon. That said, the logging road portion of this trail was a little boring, but that's fine. Because the payoff was an epic view of Lake Superior and Grand Marais from the top of a massive bald monolith. Pro tip: Make sure you veer off this loop to check out Barrier Falls. We went down to the bridge at West Devil Track before turning around and heading back to the loop. The climb out of there was a bit of a b----, but suck it up, buttercup. You've got a maple syrup latte to burn off. After this hike, we walked around Grand Marais — a charming little harbor town. We stopped by the Gunflint Tavern for lunch. But heads up, it is not dog friendly except for the upstairs bar, which does not serve food. It does, however, serve the Fulton 300 IPA, which is 10/10 if you're into that sort of thing. If you find yourself in Grand Marais, do yourself a favor and make the windy walk out to the lighthouse. I can't believe I'm saying this, but it was so cold out there that I cursed myself for not bringing a beanie. In July! Grand Marais is just about 35 miles to the Canadian border. However, my husband and I did not go to Canada. Because we are PATRIOTS. Just kidding. It's because both of our passports are expired. But we plan to remedy that soon. On our way out of town, we noticed Voyageur Brewing Company. It looked like a fun spot, and I wish we would have known about it ahead of time. They have a blonde ale that's very popular around these parts. One cool thing about the North Shore is that everything is right off US 61. You really can't get lost. So on our way back to Tofte, we stopped for a quick 1-miler at Cascade River State Park. This is an easy little trek — even after you enjoyed a beer or three in Grand Marais. Ask me how I know. The Minnesota North Shore surpassed our expectations The next morning, I set my alarm for 5 a.m. so that I could catch the sunrise. With a perfectly east-facing condo right on Lake Superior, it'd be criminal if I didn't drag my butt up for one sunrise. And, friends, it was so, so worth it. On our way back to Minocqua, we popped in Coho Cafe & Bakery. No exaggeration — the best pancakes I'd ever tasted in my life. Absolute perfection. As we enjoyed our breakfast, we plotted next year's adventure. Grand Portage, Thunder Bay, Devil's Kettle, the Summit Express gondola up Lutsen Mountain, the Boundary Waters. All the things we just didn't have time for this year. And all dog friendly. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Truthfully, we fell in love with Grand Marais. That seems like an obvious base camp for the 2027 Great White North adventure. And I promise — this time — we're hitting Betty's Pies. Love all things adventure and outdoors? Follow OutKick OutDoors on Instagram and TikTok!

articles.title: In 2017, MrBeast spent more than 40 hours counting to 100,000 on camera; years later, his video productions employ over 1,000 people
articles.summary: US Streamers News: At 13, Jimmy Donaldson was already uploading videos to YouTube. The early years were not exactly glamorous. He posted hundreds of videos and often got.
articles.body: At 13, Jimmy Donaldson was already uploading videos to YouTube. The early years were not exactly glamorous. He posted hundreds of videos and often got very few views. He and other creators also spent time studying the platform, looking at audience retention, the algorithm and thumbnail design. That obsession with how YouTube worked became part of the foundation for what came next. Then came January 2017, when Donaldson decided to do something that sounds ridiculous on paper. He started counting to 100,000 on camera. The filming did not take a few hours. It went on for 40 straight hours. Donaldson later explained that he wanted to binge-watch Game of Thrones and Naruto, but felt guilty about spending that time without earning money. Counting let him do both.The 40-hour stunt had a weird reason behind itThe finished upload is not the full 40-hour recording. It runs for 23 hours and 48 minutes because his editing software had a 24-hour maximum. Several parts of the footage were sped up to fit under that limit.The stunt also got a major boost from other creators. Members of FaZe Clan reacted to the video in their vlogs, helping make it his first major traffic driver. Donaldson then followed it with other unusual endurance ideas, including reading the dictionary and watching paint dry.His YouTube operation grew far beyond a bedroom setupAs the channel expanded, Donaldson started putting nearly all his earnings back into videos. Simple room challenges gave way to elaborate productions, large cash giveaways and sets that required far more people to build and run.That operation now sits under Beast Industries, a parent holding company with more than 1,000 people across full-time staff, contracted construction crews, set designers and specialized security teams. Production takes place on a 100-acre corporate compound with multiple multi-million-dollar soundstages designed for indoor sets.The production budget is huge too. Donaldson has said roughly $250 million a year goes into content creation. A standard video shoot can cost more than $1 million, and he has even scrapped completed million-dollar videos when he felt the final cut was not entertaining enough.The creator also built businesses outside YouTubeThe expansion did not stop with videos. Feastables became a snack brand, while Lunchly entered the packaged lunch market. Beast Industries also acquired Step, a financial app focused on teaching teens investing and asset management. Its team also developed Viewstats, a YouTube analytics platform built to optimize content performance.Then came mainstream television. Amazon signed a deal worth more than $100 million for Beast Games on Prime Video. Beast Industries also closed a $200 million funding round at a $5 billion valuation.That makes the 2017 counting video look very different in hindsight. It was a 40-hour stunt built around one creator and a strange idea. Years later, the same creator's content operation involves giant sets, seven-figure shoots and more than 1,000 people working across the business behind the scenes, across production and the company.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: UK heatwave exposes 300-year-old hidden gardens  as drought reveals forgotten historic landscapes across Europe
articles.summary: UK News: Britain’s scorching summer is doing more than turning lawns brown. Across parts of the UK, prolonged heat and unusually dry conditions are causing his.
articles.body: Britain’s scorching summer is doing more than turning lawns brown. Across parts of the UK, prolonged heat and unusually dry conditions are causing historic patterns buried beneath layers of soil and turf to reappear, offering archaeologists and historians a fleeting glimpse into landscapes that disappeared centuries ago. From the formal gardens of Chatsworth to a long-lost design at Blenheim Palace, parched grass is acting almost like a natural archaeological scanner. The phenomenon occurs because grass growing above old paths, walls and flowerbeds often has shallower roots than plants growing over deeper, undisturbed soil. When temperatures rise and rainfall disappears, those areas dry out faster, leaving contrasting marks across the landscape. What looks like damaged grass can therefore become a remarkable map of Britain's hidden past.How extreme heat is exposing Britain's buried historyThe discovery begins with a simple difference beneath the surface. Historic gardens were often constructed using gravel paths, stonework, compacted ground and densely planted flowerbeds. Even after these features were removed and lawns were laid over them, the buried structures continued to influence the soil above. During prolonged hot and dry weather, that difference becomes visible. Grass growing over compacted paths or former planting beds has less access to moisture and can turn yellow or brown sooner than grass rooted in deeper soil. The result is a pattern of lines, curves and geometric shapes that can correspond remarkably closely with historic maps and archaeological records. At Chatsworth in Derbyshire, recent record temperatures and long dry periods have exposed the outline of the Great Parterre on the South Lawn. According to Chatsworth, the elaborate ornamental garden was created for the 1st Duke of Devonshire around 1699 before being covered over and replaced with another design around 1730. The estate says the grass planted over the former paths and flowerbeds has shorter roots, meaning it burns more rapidly during hot, dry conditions. That temporary difference has brought the swirling pattern of the 17th-century garden back into view.Chatsworth's lost garden returns beneath the scorched lawnThe Great Parterre was not a small decorative patch. It was an elaborate formal garden measuring about 473 by 227 feet, filled with patterned flowerbeds and paths designed to complement the newly created south façade of Chatsworth House. Its disappearance was part of the changing fashions of British landscape gardening. The formal design was eventually covered and replaced, but the archaeological footprint remained beneath the lawn. Now, the weather has effectively recreated a ghost image of the garden. Chatsworth's own historical records show that similar parch marks have appeared during previous periods of extreme heat. The estate recorded particularly clear outlines of the 1st Duke's parterre during the 2022 heatwave, when temperatures reached 38.1°C at Chatsworth. The estate has also recorded a longer-term shift towards sunnier springs and prolonged dry periods, conditions that can make these archaeological traces easier to see. The discovery demonstrates why drought can sometimes provide an unexpected archaeological advantage. Features that would normally remain invisible from ground level can suddenly become obvious from above, allowing researchers to compare the patterns with historic drawings and surviving records.A 300-year-old garden appears at Blenheim PalaceThe phenomenon has also produced a striking discovery at Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire, where dry conditions have revealed the footprint of a garden that disappeared from the landscape centuries ago. The garden was dismantled in the 1760s, but its buried archaeological remains survived beneath the modern lawn. As the grass dried, the former layout began appearing as a large-scale pattern across the ground. Blenheim is not the only historic landscape where extreme weather has exposed traces of the past. Similar archaeological marks can reveal former buildings, paths, military structures and settlements because buried features alter how water is stored and absorbed by the soil. Andy Mills, head gardener at Blenheim Palace, told the BBC that the garden's footprint had appeared across the lawn and described the scale of the discovery as extraordinary. He said the archaeological remains were already known to exist beneath the ground, but the unusually hot weather had created an unexpected opportunity to see them. The discovery is particularly valuable because historic gardens can be substantially altered by later generations. At Chatsworth, for example, the removal of the earlier formal gardens in the 1730s transformed the appearance of the estate, while surviving records and archaeological traces preserve evidence of what came before.Heatwaves are turning Britain's lawns into temporary archaeological mapsThe sudden appearance of these patterns highlights an unusual relationship between extreme weather and archaeology. The same dry conditions that stress vegetation can expose structures that have remained hidden for hundreds of years. And the clues are not limited to gardens. Across Britain, aerial surveys and drought-related changes have also helped reveal traces of historic settlements and military sites. The recent discoveries include the remains of the lost village of Nether Hambleton as water levels fell at Rutland Water, while aerial imagery has identified wartime features in Wales. For archaeologists, timing is crucial. Once rainfall returns and vegetation recovers, the patterns can disappear again, leaving only photographs, aerial surveys and historical records behind. That makes every heatwave an unusual window into the past. Beneath an ordinary lawn may be the outline of a forgotten garden, an old pathway or even an entire lost settlement. When the soil dries enough, those buried histories can briefly rise to the surface, not because anything new has been built, but because the landscape has finally revealed what was there all along.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
